thread.title: Microsoft Is Challenging Apple to Be the Most Valuable Company. But Beware the 'Winner's Curse.'

title: Microsoft Is Challenging Apple to Be the Most Valuable Company. But Beware the 'Winner's Curse.'
text:
Microsoft Could Beat Apple as the Most Valuable Company. But the ‘Winner’s Curse’ Looms. By Updated Nov. 29, 2018 9:37 a.m. ET Order Reprints Photo by Gerard Julien/AFP/Getty Images Text size
Apple stock (AAPL) has tumbled in recent weeks while Microsoft stock (MSFT) has held fairly steady —and the two giants are suddenly neck and neck for the title of largest company by market value.
That should give Microsoft shareholders pause.
There’s a well-known tendency of companies that reach the top spot by market value to underperform for years afterward. But even more important than trend is the likely cause behind it. Rob Arnott has studied “The Winners Curse ” for the broad U.S. market, individual sectors, and overseas markets. He found in each case that top dogs earn lousy 10-year returns. In the U.S. market, for example, there were six leaders between 1952 and 2010, and they underperformed by a whopping five percentage points per year in the decade after taking the top spot.
Arnott has skin in the game as founder and chairman of Research Affiliates, which markets investment indexes that weight companies by economic factors, not market value. The thinking is that a high stock value is a negative predictor of future returns, while high earnings, revenues, dividends, and so on are not. The firm says its approach to indexing is thus superior to tracking indexes like the S&P 500 .
Apple kept the top spot Wednesday , with Apple stock closing up 3.9% for a market capitalization of about $858 billion. Microsoft stock closed up 3.7%, to end the day at a market value if about $852 billion.
In his 2012 study, Arnott considered a handful of possible explanations for The Winner’s Curse. The top companies in their fields can attract unwanted regulation, antitrust action, and public scorn. “Being #1 means always having to say you’re sorry!” Arnott wrote in the Journal of Indexes . Stock market leaders also get lots of media coverage, and prior research has shown that to be an undesirable thing for returns. But the most plausible explanation, as Arnott put it, is that “a high price is often needed to get to the vaunted #1 rank by market cap.”
Read our recent cover story : The tornado in tech stocks
The existence of a common-sense explanation for The Winner’s Curse is important because the sample size of leaders to study isn’t huge, and there are exceptions to the rule. Exxon Mobil (XOM) has been a poor performer over the past decade, but it has been hanging around the U.S. market’s top 10 list for more than a half-century, so its size hasn’t historically been a hindrance. In data going back to 1981, it has traded at an average of 14 times trailing earnings—reasonable enough to suggest a lofty valuation hasn’t been much of a hindrance, either. Compare that with Microsoft, which went for more than 60 times earnings in September 1998, when it topped General Electric (GE) to become the largest U.S. company. Over the following decade, it returned about half as much as the market.
Microsoft isn’t nearly that expensive today. But it isn’t cheap either. Barron’s wrote favorably about the company more than three years ago. Microsoft stock has returned 155% since, including dividends, trouncing the market by more than 100 points. But consider that while Microsoft and Apple are close in market value, they are far apart in economic output. Apple is expected to clear more than $63 billion in free cash in its current fiscal year through Sep. 2019, compared to about $36 billion for Microsoft in its fiscal year ending June 2019.
Based on free cash projections, Microsoft has risen from a 29% discount to the S&P 500 at the time of our 2015 story, to a recent 16% premium. Apple, meanwhile, traded recently at a 38% discount. Microsoft is seen as the faster grower of the two, with Wall Street looking for three-year, compounded earnings per share growth averaging 15%, versus 11% for Apple. But if The Winner’s Curse is owed more to valuation than just size, Microsoft shareholders should be more concerned from here about having regained the top spot than Apple investors should be about losing it.
